title: Can the Meroitic language be translated beyond its funerary formulae?
short: Meroitic script has been readable since Griffith's work of 1909–1911, but outside formulaic texts the language of the Kingdom of Kush is still largely untranslated.
matters: Meroitic is the oldest written language of sub-Saharan Africa and the administrative and royal language of Kush for some seven centuries. The long royal stelae, temple texts and chronicles almost certainly record wars with Rome, succession and religious practice from a Kushite point of view; at present historians rely on Greek, Latin and Egyptian sources for that history. A secure classification would also date the spread of Northern East Sudanic languages along the Nile, which bears on Nubian linguistic and population history.
stuck: The script's sound values were recovered from Egyptian names, but there is no substantial bilingual text, and the language has no close, well-documented descendant. Most of the corpus consists of funerary inscriptions with predictable formulae, so the vocabulary securely understood is small, by most accounts on the order of a hundred words, and grammar is reconstructed mainly from those formulae. Classification is disputed: Rilly argues for the Northern East Sudanic branch with Nubian, Nara, Taman and Nyima, while Rowan and Lipiński have argued for an Afroasiatic affiliation.
solved: A lexicon and grammar, fixed before testing, yield translations of held-out non-funerary passages (for example sections of royal stelae or temple texts) that independent specialists judge consistent with their archaeological, iconographic and historical context, and that correctly predict content later confirmed by newly found or newly published inscriptions.
approach: Convert the REM corpus and inscriptions published since 2000 into a machine-readable, lemmatized corpus with find context, object type and date.

Use reconstructed Proto-Northern East Sudanic and Old Nubian vocabulary to generate constrained translation hypotheses, and test them against held-out passages whose context (offering scenes, lists of places, military iconography) predicts parts of the content.

Comparative work needs collaboration with Nubian and Nilo-Saharan linguists, and the corpus needs digitization of inscriptions excavated after 2000 and photographs held by excavation missions, given reported damage to collections in Khartoum during the war that began in 2023.

existing.authors: David Randall-MacIver and C. Leonard Woolley, with F. Ll. Griffith
existing.title: Areika
existing.venue: Eckley B. Coxe Junior Expedition to Nubia 1. Oxford: University Museum
existing.note: Excavation report including Griffith's first presentation of the Meroitic sign values, worked out from Meroitic spellings of Egyptian names.

existing.title: Karanòg: The Meroitic Inscriptions of Shablûl and Karanòg
existing.venue: Eckley B. Coxe Junior Expedition to Nubia 6. Philadelphia: University Museum
existing.note: Edition of the funerary inscriptions from two Lower Nubian cemeteries, with Griffith's analysis of the formulae and a first sketch of the language.

existing.title: Spoken and Written Meroitic: A Note on the Terminal Formulae in Meroitic Funerary Inscriptions from Armenna West
existing.note: Used variation in funerary formulae to infer features of the spoken language behind the written conventions.

existing.authors: Jean Leclant, André Heyler, Catherine Berger-el Naggar, Claude Carrier and Claude Rilly
existing.title: Répertoire d'épigraphie méroïtique (REM), tomes I–III
existing.venue: Paris: Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres
existing.note: Corpus of all Meroitic inscriptions published to that date, numbered REM 0001 to 1278, now openly available on Persée.

existing.title: Recent Research on Meroitic, the Ancient Language of Sudan
existing.note: Survey of the corpus (about 90 per cent cursive), its chronology and the comparative case for Northern East Sudanic affiliation.

existing.authors: Claude Rilly and Alex de Voogt
existing.title: The Meroitic Language and Writing System
existing.note: English-language reference grammar and script description summarizing Rilly's La langue du royaume de Méroé (2007) and Le méroïtique et sa famille linguistique (2010).

existing.title: The Meroitic 'Initial a' Sign as Griffith's Initial Aleph
existing.venue: Zeitschrift für Ägyptische Sprache und Altertumskunde 142 (1): 70–84
existing.note: Part of Rowan's phonological reanalysis of the script, which underlies her argument that Meroitic phonotactics fit an Afroasiatic language better than an East Sudanic one.

existing.title: Languages of Ancient Nubia
existing.venue: In Dietrich Raue (ed.), Handbook of Ancient Nubia. Berlin: De Gruyter, 129–152
existing.note: Places Meroitic among the attested and inferred languages of the Middle Nile, including Old Nubian and earlier Kushite names in Egyptian sources.

existing.title: Personal Markers and Verbal Number in Meroitic
existing.venue: Dotawo: A Journal of Nubian Studies 7
existing.note: Reconstructs verbal morphology through comparison with Nubian and other Northern East Sudanic languages, the main route by which grammar beyond the formulae has advanced.

existing.title: Morphological Evidence for the Coherence of East Sudanic
existing.venue: Dotawo: A Journal of Nubian Studies 7: 264–311
existing.note: Assesses whether East Sudanic is a valid genetic unit, the comparative frame on which Rilly's classification of Meroitic depends.

existing.title: Language and Writing in the Kingdom of Meroe
existing.venue: In Geoff Emberling and Bruce Beyer Williams (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Ancient Nubia. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 653–669
existing.note: Current overview of what can and cannot be translated, with the state of the lexicon and the main unread text genres.

archives.repository: Persée / Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres
archives.note: Open scanned corpus with transliterations and bibliography; not lemmatized or machine-structured, and it stops at 2000.

holdings.name: Répertoire d'épigraphie méroïtique, Tome I
holdings.note: First volume of the printed corpus (Leclant et al., 2000), with texts and bibliography; Tomes II and III continue to REM 1278.

archives.collection: Department of Egypt and Sudan: Meroitic inscriptions, including the long stela of Amanirenas and Akinidad from Hamadab
archives.note: Online collection records with images for many objects; the Hamadab stela is one of the longest non-funerary Meroitic texts.

holdings.name: Hamadab stela of Amanirenas and Akinidad
holdings.note: Sandstone stela excavated by Garstang in 1914, with 42 lines of Meroitic cursive, among the longest known texts; its twin was left at Hamadab.

archives.collection: Eckley B. Coxe Junior Expedition to Nubia: inscribed offering tables and stelae from Karanog, Shablul and Areika
archives.note: Holds much of the material Griffith used to establish the script, with excavation records.

holdings.name: Offering table from Karanog
holdings.note: Meroitic funerary offering table from the Karanog cemetery, typical of the formulaic texts that dominate the corpus.

holdings.name: Griffith, Karanòg: the Meroitic inscriptions of Shablûl and Karanòg (1911)
holdings.ref: Eckley B. Coxe Junior Expedition to Nubia 6
holdings.note: Digitized edition of the Karanog and Shablul texts on which Griffith based his decipherment.

archives.collection: Harvard University–Boston Museum of Fine Arts Expedition finds from the royal cemeteries of Meroe and other Kushite sites
archives.note: Royal and elite inscribed objects with excavation context from Reisner's expedition; online records vary in completeness.

holdings.name: Offering table of King Amanitaraqide
holdings.note: Offering table excavated in 1921 at Meroe N 16 with Meroitic text around the perimeter; reference taken from a search snippet of the MFA record, which could not be opened.

archives.repository: Ägyptisches Museum und Papyrussammlung, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin
archives.collection: Meroitic inscriptions and objects from the Lepsius expedition and later German work at Naga and Musawwarat es-Sufra
archives.note: Searchable through SMB-digital; includes temple and royal inscriptions as well as funerary material.
